qs.q: Which spirometric finding is characteristic of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)?
o: Increased FEV1 to FVC ratio
Decreased expiratory flow rate
Elevated total lung capacity
Markedly increased forced vital capacity
qs.e: COPD is characterized by a decreased expiratory flow rate and a decreased FEV1 to FVC ratio below 0.70. Total lung capacity is usually normal or increased due to air trapping.
qs.s: Dr. Irungu Sent SEM 2 — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following best defines the pulmonary component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)?
o: Airflow limitation that is fully reversible with bronchodilators
Airflow limitation that is not fully reversible and progressive
Fixed airway obstruction exclusively caused by extensive fibrosis
Acute episodic bronchoconstriction triggered solely by allergies
qs.e: COPD is characterized by airflow limitation that is not fully reversible and is progressive, associated with an abnormal inflammatory response. Unlike asthma, the limitation does not reverse completely.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: A 55-year-old heavy cigarette smoker presents with progressive shortness of breath. According to the epidemiological and aetiological data, what is considered the usual minimum smoking history to develop COPD?
o: Less than five accumulated pack-years of tobacco use
At least ten accumulated pack-years of tobacco use
Exactly two accumulated pack-years of tobacco use
No measurable pack-years of prior tobacco exposure
qs.e: Cigarette smoking is the most significant cause of COPD, and it is unusual to develop the condition with less than 10 pack-years. Reducing cigarette numbers has little impact, but complete cessation alters the disease course.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: In addition to tobacco smoking, which of the following indoor environmental exposures is a well-recognized major risk factor for developing COPD, particularly in low- and middle-income countries?
o: Biomass solid fuel fires such as wood and animal dung
Prolonged exposure to residential natural gas heaters
Frequent use of synthetic chemical aerosol air fresheners
High levels of indoor ultraviolet radiation exposure
qs.e: Biomass solid fuel fires including wood, animal dung, crop residues, and coal lead to high levels of indoor air pollution and serve as major risk factors for COPD. Tobacco smoke remains the primary global cause.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old patient with advanced COPD presents with peripheral oedema and morning headaches. Which underlying physiological abnormality is most strongly suggested by these symptoms?
o: Severe chronic hypercapnia affecting renal excretion
Isolated left ventricular failure with fluid retention
Primary hyperparathyroidism causing systemic edema
Acute renal tubular necrosis with electrolyte loss
qs.e: In advanced disease, oedema and morning headaches may suggest hypercapnia. Oedema usually relates to the failure of salt and water excretion by the hypoxic, hypercapnic kidney.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: Which classical clinical phenotype of COPD describes a patient who is typically thin, breathless, and maintains a normal arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) until late in the disease?
o: Pink puffer phenotype maintaining normal carbon dioxide
Blue bloater phenotype with early carbon dioxide retention
Atopic bronchitic phenotype with prominent eosinophilia
Hypersecretory asthmatic phenotype with variable obstruction
qs.e: Pink puffers are typically thin and breathless and maintain a normal PaCO2 until the late stage of disease. In contrast, blue bloaters develop or tolerate hypercapnia earlier and may develop oedema.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: Which diagnostic investigation is essential to confirm the diagnosis of COPD by demonstrating airflow obstruction?
o: Diagnostic spirometry demonstrating fixed airflow limitation
Standard chest radiography evaluating hyperinflation signs
Body plethysmography measuring absolute lung capacities
High-resolution computed tomography detecting bullae
qs.e: The diagnosis of COPD is confirmed by demonstrating airflow obstruction by spirometry. While chest X-rays and HRCT are useful for identifying alternative diagnoses and bullae, they do not establish airflow limitation.
qs.s: 3.CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE(COPD) MKU PPT (1): MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary reason why body plethysmography is preferred over the helium dilution technique when measuring lung volumes in patients with severe COPD?
o: Helium dilution may underestimate volumes in large bullae
Body plethysmography exposes patients to lower radiation
Helium gas is highly toxic to inflamed bronchial mucosa
Body plethysmography directly measures diffusing capacity
qs.e: In severe COPD, and in particular with large bullae, body plethysmography is preferred because the use of helium may underestimate lung volumes. Helium struggles to equilibrate fully within poorly communicating bullous spaces.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: COPD is a progressive lung disease causing airflow limitation. It's primarily linked to smoking and environmental irritants. Management focuses on symptom relief, reducing exacerbations, and slowing disease progression.

sections.p: COPD is a progressive, largely irreversible airflow limitation, often associated with chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Diagnosis is suspected in patients with chronic respiratory symptoms and a history of exposure to noxious particles, especially smoking. Spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 confirms the diagnosis.
b: Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnoea.
A history of significant exposure to risk factors is crucial.

sections.p: Severity is assessed by symptom burden, exacerbation frequency, and spirometric findings. The GOLD system categorises COPD into stages based on FEV1 and symptom scores (CAT or mMRC).

The most common cause is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke. Other significant causes include biomass fuel exposure (indoor air pollution), occupational dusts and chemicals, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Patients typically present with chronic cough, often worse in the morning, sputum production, and progressive shortness of breath, especially on exertion. Exacerbations are acute worsening of symptoms.

t.b: Confirms airflow limitation and aids diagnosis. A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.7 indicates COPD.
Excludes other causes of symptoms like pneumonia or lung cancer. May show hyperinflation or flattened diaphragms in COPD.
Assesses oxygenation and ventilation, especially in moderate to severe COPD or during exacerbations. Hypoxia and hypercapnia may be present.

sections.p: Acute exacerbations, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, and respiratory failure are serious complications. A sudden increase in dyspnoea or chest pain warrants urgent assessment.

Management aims to reduce symptoms, decrease exacerbation frequency, and improve exercise tolerance. Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention. Pharmacological treatment includes bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids. Pulmonary rehabilitation is vital.
Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease progression, adjust treatment, and manage exacerbations. Prevention focuses on smoking cessation and avoiding exposure to irritants.
COPD can be mistaken for asthma, heart failure, bronchiectasis, and interstitial lung disease due to overlapping symptoms like dyspnoea and cough.
Spirometry may be normal in very early disease. ABGs can appear normal at rest in patients with moderate COPD, only showing abnormalities with exertion or during exacerbations.
b: Normal ABGs at rest in stable COPD
Pulse oximetry may not reflect severe hypoxemia in some cases.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of shortness of breath
Bluish discoloration of lips or face

faq.q: What is the main cause of COPD?
faq.a: The most common cause is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke.
COPD cannot be cured, but its progression can be slowed and symptoms managed effectively.

faq.q: What is an exacerbation of COPD?
faq.a: An exacerbation is a sudden worsening of COPD symptoms, often requiring increased medication or hospitalization.
